[[File:Claytone de Cuba2.jpg|thumb|Illustration of Claytone de Cuba (''Claytonia perfoliata'') in "Les Plantes potagères" Vilmorin 1925]]
'''''Claytonia perfoliata''''', commonly known as '''miner's lettuce''' or '''winter purslane''', is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Montiaceae]]. It is an edible, fleshy, [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]], [[annual plant]] native to the western [[mountain]] and [[coast]]al regions of North America.

==Description==
''Claytonia perfoliata'' is a tender [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]]-forming plant that grows to some {{Convert|30|cm|abbr=off}} in height,{{r|ediblewildplants2009}} but mature plants can be as short as {{Convert|1|cm||abbr=on|frac=8}}. The [[cotyledon]]s are usually bright green (rarely purplish- or brownish-green), [[succulent]], long and narrow. The first [[true leaves]] form a rosette at the base of the plant, and are {{Convert|0.5|to|4|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, with a typically long [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] (exceptionally up to {{Convert|20|cm||abbr=on|disp=or|frac=2}} long).

The small pink or white [[flower]]s have five [[Petals of a flower|petals]] {{convert|2|to|6|mm|frac=16}} long. The flowers appear from February to May or June and are grouped 5–40 together. The flowers grow above a pair of leaves that are connected together around the stem so as to appear as a single circular leaf. Mature plants form a rosette; they have numerous erect to spreading stems that branch from the base.

''C. perfoliata'' is common in the springtime, and prefers a cool, damp environment. The plant first appears in sunlit areas after the first heavy rains of the year, though the best stands are found in shaded areas, especially in the [[Upland and lowland|uplands]], into early summer. As the days get hotter and drier, the leaves [[Autumn leaf color|turn a deep red color]] as they dry out.

==Taxonomy==
Together with two other ''[[Claytonia]]'' species, ''[[Claytonia parviflora]]'' and ''[[Claytonia rubra|C. rubra]]'', ''C. perfoliata'' comprises what is almost certainly a [[polyploid]] pillar complex,{{r|mcintyre2012cytogeo}} which is based on three [[Diploid|diploid species]].{{r|miller2006}}  Two key [[Scientific studies|studies]] on the [[population ecology]] and [[Population genetics|genetics]] of the ''C. perfoliata'' [[Species complex|complex]] were published in 2012.{{r|mcintyre2012cytogeo}}{{r|mcintyre2012polyploidy}}

=== Subspecies ===
There are three well-studied geographical [[subspecies]] of ''C. perfoliata'':{{r|miller2006}}
* ''Claytonia perfoliata'' subsp. ''perfoliata'': [[Pacific coast|Pacific coastal United States]] and Canada ([[British Columbia]])
* ''Claytonia perfoliata'' subsp. ''intermontana'': interior [[western United States]]
* ''Claytonia perfoliata'' subsp. ''mexicana'': coastal [[southern California]] and Arizona, all the way south to Mexico to Guatemala

===Names===
The genus ''Claytonia'' is named in honor of the American botanist [[John_Clayton_(botanist)|John Clayton]].<ref name=plantnamesexplained2024/>{{rp|p=54}} The [[Specific_name_(zoology)|specific epithet]] ''perfoliata'' means [[perfoliate]].<ref name=plantnamesexplained2024/>{{rp|p=157}}

The [[common name]] ''miner's lettuce'' is attributed to the use of ''Claytonia perfoliata'' during the [[California gold rush]],<ref name="Linford">{{cite book |last1=Linford |first1=Jenny |title=A Concise Guide to Herbs |date=2007 |publisher=Parragon |location=Bath, England |isbn=978-1-4054-8799-3 |page=88 |url=https://archive.org/details/conciseguidetohe0000unse/page/88 |access-date=7 April 2025}}</ref> however its first known use in print does not occur until 1921 in the writings of [[Gene Stratton-Porter]].<ref>{{Cite OED|Miner's Lettuce, N. |3833988721}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Stratton-Porter |first1=Gene |author1-link=Gene Stratton-Porter |title=Her Father's Daughter |date=1921 |publisher=Grosset & Dunlap |location=New York |page=79 |url=https://archive.org/details/herfathersdaugh00stragoog/page/n82 |access-date=7 April 2025}}</ref> The name ''winter purslane'' first occurs earlier in 1884 in the ''Dictionary of English Names of Plants'' by William Miller.<ref>{{Cite OED|Winter Purslane, N. |8810665888}}</ref>

''C. perfoliata'' is called 'piyada̠' in the [[Mono language (California)|Western Mono language]] and 'palsingat' in [[Cahuilla language|Ivilyuat]] — two Native American languages of California<ref>[http://northforkrancheria-nsn.gov/home/showdocument?id=29 "A Dictionary of Western Mono: Second Edition"]</ref> or 'rooreh' in ([[Ohlone languages|Ohlone language]])<ref>{{Citation |title=rooreh |date=2020-09-06 |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/w/index.php?title=rooreh&oldid=60308776 |work=Wiktionary |access-date=2023-04-28 |language=en}}</ref> The name Rooreh has been adopted by the [[University and Jepson Herbaria|Jepson Herbarium]] at [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Claytonia perfoliata |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=19632, |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=ucjeps.berkeley.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-01 |title=November 2024: Rooreh |url=https://aclibrary.org/blogs/post/november-2024-rooreh/ |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=aclibrary.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The species is native to Mexico and western north America as far north as British Columbia.<ref name=powo>{{cite web |work=Plants of the World Online | publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |title=''Claytonia perfoliata'' Donn. ex Willd. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:60021-2 |access-date=28 April 2023 }}</ref> 

It has been introduced into and is widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in [[western Europe]], Argentina and New Zealand<ref name=powo/> It was introduced to Europe in the 18th century, possibly by the [[naturalist]] [[Archibald Menzies]], who brought it to [[Kew Gardens]] in London in 1794.{{r|atlantic11}}{{r|menzies1792}} It was first recorded in the wild in Britain in South Hampshire in 1849 and is still spreading.<ref name=BSBIAtlas2020>{{cite web |title=''Claytonia perfoliata'' Donn ex Willd. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5= D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.brd |access-date=28 April 2023 }}</ref>

As of 2019 sightings of this plant have been found as far inland as Arkansas.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schneider |first=Adam C. |title=''Claytonia Perfoliata'' (Montiaceae) Newly Reported In Arkansas, U.S.A. |date= October 2019 |journal=Journal of the Botanical Research Institute of Texas |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=495–497 |doi=10.17348/jbrit.v13.i2.806 |jstor=26844050 |s2cid=244520656 |issn=1934-5259|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Salade de pourpier.JPG|thumb|Miner's lettuce served as a salad]]

The [[common name]] of ''miner's lettuce'' refers to how the plant was used by [[miner]]s during the [[California Gold Rush]], who ate it to prevent [[scurvy]].{{r|ernesttop100_2014}}{{r|note1}}{{r|note2}} It is in season in April and May, and can be eaten as a [[leaf vegetable]].{{r|lyons1956}} The entire plant is edible, except the roots, and it provides [[vitamin C]].{{r|foragingedibleplants2016}} Most commonly, it is eaten [[Raw food|raw]] in [[salad]]s, but it is not quite as delicate as [[Cultigen|cultivated]] [[lettuce]]. Sometimes, it is [[boiled]] like [[spinach]], which it resembles in taste and chemical composition. Caution should be used because wild ''C. perfoliata'' can sometimes accumulate [[Toxicity|toxic]] amounts of [[sodium oxalate]] (as can happen in spinach).{{R|UCD}}

The plant is known as ''palsingat'' or, possibly, ''lahchumeek'' in [[Cahuilla language|Ivilyuat]] and it was eaten fresh or boiled as a green by the [[Cahuilla|Ivilyuqaletem]] (Cahuilla) people  of Southern California. It, along with ''[[Claytonia exigua]]'', is available for gathering in the early spring.{{r|temalpakh}}
